title: SHE WAS PHARAOH’S DAUGHTER… BUT HER NAME WAS WRITTEN INTO ISRAEL’S STORY.
paragraphs: SHE WAS PHARAOH’S DAUGHTER… BUT HER NAME WAS WRITTEN INTO ISRAEL’S STORY.

An Egyptian princess appeared in the family records of God's people. Her name was Bithiah, meaning “Daughter of Yahweh.” And behind that extraordinary name is a truth about grace, identity, and belonging that reaches all the way to Jesus Christ.
What if the name the world gave you was not the name that would define your eternity?
Imagine being born into a palace where your father was called Pharaoh.
You grew up surrounded by the symbols of Egyptian royalty. You belonged to a dynasty associated with power, wealth, and a civilization whose history included the oppression of Israel.
And then, centuries later, someone opens the sacred genealogies of Israel and discovers your name.
Not merely as an Egyptian.
Not merely as a princess.
But as a woman remembered within an Israelite family.
And the name recorded beside you means something astonishing.
Daughter of Yahweh.
Her name was Bithiah.
And although Scripture gives us only a brief glimpse of her life, that glimpse is enough to make us ask a question that reaches into our own hearts.
What happens when the identity you inherited is no longer the deepest truth about who you are?

Perhaps you were born into a family where faith was absent. Perhaps you grew up carrying the shame of decisions you never made. Perhaps your past has followed you so relentlessly that you have begun to believe you can never become anything different.
Or perhaps you have spent years building a respectable life while secretly wondering whether God would still welcome you if everyone knew the whole story.
Then stay with this account.
Because buried inside a genealogy most people hurry past is a woman's name that invites us to think about the extraordinary mercy of God.
And before we finish, we must confront something even more important than the mystery of an Egyptian princess.
We must confront the question of what it truly means to belong to God.
The passage is found in 1 Chronicles 4:17–18.
These verses appear in a section of Scripture filled with family names, marriages, and descendants. At first glance, they seem almost impossible to turn into a memorable story.
But suddenly, in the middle of the genealogy, a remarkable identification appears.
The King James Version records the closing portion of verse 18 this way:
“And these are the sons of Bithiah the daughter of Pharaoh, which Mered took.”
Read those words again.
Bithiah the daughter of Pharaoh.
Which Mered took.

The Hebrew verb translated “took” is לָקַח (laqach), a word that can describe taking someone in marriage. The context supports the understanding that Mered, an Israelite man listed in Judah's genealogical records, married Bithiah.
The preceding lines also refer to Mered's Jewish wife, although the exact arrangement of the family relationships in these difficult Hebrew verses is debated.
What is unmistakable is this:
An Egyptian woman identified as Pharaoh's daughter was remembered by name in the genealogical record of Judah.
We are not told which Pharaoh was her father.
We are not told precisely when she lived.
We are not told how she met Mered, why she entered his household, or what personal decisions led to her place in this genealogy.
And we must be careful not to invent what God has not revealed.
Scripture does not record a dramatic escape from the palace, a secret conversion ceremony, or a confrontation between Bithiah and her father.
Those might make compelling scenes in a historical novel.
But they are not facts established by 1 Chronicles.
The biblical account is already remarkable without adding imaginary details.
Because there is something extraordinary about the name itself.
In Hebrew, Bithiah is written בִּתְיָה (Bityah).
The name is commonly understood to mean “Daughter of Yahweh” or “Daughter of the LORD.”
The first element is related to the Hebrew word for daughter, בַּת (bat). The second element, יָהּ (Yah), is a shortened form of the divine name.
Consider the contrast.
Scripture identifies her by her earthly father.
But the name Scripture preserves speaks of the LORD.
Pharaoh's daughter.
Daughter of Yahweh.
Two descriptions appearing in the story of one woman.

We cannot prove from the name alone exactly when she received it, whether she was given it at birth, or whether it reflected a personal conversion to Israel's God. Jewish interpretive tradition later associated her with a profound act of identification with God's people, but those traditions must be distinguished from what the biblical text explicitly says.
Still, the name itself invites reflection.
Because every human being lives with more than one description.
There is the identity others assign to us.
The family we came from.
The failures people remember.
The reputation we cannot seem to escape.
The wounds we hide.
The labels spoken over us when we were too young to understand their weight.
And then there is the question that matters more than any earthly title.
Who does God say we are?
Maybe someone reading this has spent an entire lifetime trying to outrun a family history.
Your father was absent, and you promised yourself you would never become like him.
Your mother carried pain she never knew how to express, and somehow you inherited it.
Your childhood taught you that love had to be earned.
Your mistakes convinced you that acceptance was temporary.
You learned to smile when people asked how you were doing.
You learned to say, “I'm fine,” even when your heart was exhausted.
And eventually, you began to believe the worst things that happened to you were the truest things about you.
But listen carefully.
Your past can explain part of your story without having the authority to determine its ending.
That does not mean the past disappears.
It does not mean consequences vanish.
And it certainly does not mean a person becomes a child of God merely by wanting a new identity.
The Gospel tells us something far greater.
Through Jesus Christ, sinners can be forgiven, reconciled to God, and adopted into His family.
John 1:12 declares:
“But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name.” — KJV
The Greek word translated “power” here is ἐξουσία (exousia), conveying the right or authority granted to those who receive Christ.
And the expression τέκνα θεοῦ (tekna Theou) means “children of God.”
This is not a promise that every person automatically possesses saving sonship regardless of faith.
It is a promise connected to receiving Jesus Christ and believing in His name.
That distinction matters.
Because the Christian message is not simply that everyone should feel better about themselves.
It is that sinners need a Savior.
We do not become God's children by improving our public image, accumulating religious achievements, purchasing spiritual approval, or rewriting our personal history.
We become His children through faith in Jesus Christ.
And that brings us to something deeper in Bithiah's story.
She is identified as Egyptian.
Her name is preserved in the records of Judah.
That fact should remind us that the biblical story was never merely about one ethnic people possessing a God who had no concern for the nations.
God chose Israel for His covenant purposes, and through Israel He promised blessing that would ultimately reach the nations.
Long before the birth of Jesus, the LORD told Abraham:
“And in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed.” — Genesis 12:3, KJV
Notice the scope.
All families.
Not one palace.
Not one nation.
Not one social class.
Not one generation.
All families of the earth.
That promise finds its ultimate fulfillment in Jesus Christ, the promised offspring of Abraham, through whom the blessing of salvation reaches believing Jews and Gentiles.
Galatians 3:26–29 makes the connection clear.
Those who belong to Christ through faith are Abraham's offspring and heirs according to the promise.
And suddenly the presence of an Egyptian woman in Judah's genealogy becomes a powerful occasion to reflect on God's wider redemptive purpose.
Not because Bithiah's brief record proves every detail of her spiritual journey.
It does not.
But because the larger story of Scripture repeatedly shows God's mercy reaching people whom others might have considered outsiders.
Think of Rahab.
A Canaanite woman in Jericho, identified in Scripture as a prostitute, who confessed the LORD's supremacy and acted in faith.
Her story did not end with the destruction of Jericho.
She was spared.
She lived among Israel.
And Matthew's genealogy names Rahab in the ancestral line of Jesus Christ.
Think of Ruth.
A Moabite widow who chose to identify herself with Naomi's people and Naomi's God.
She declared:
“Thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God.” — Ruth 1:16, KJV
Ruth became the great-grandmother of King David.
And through David's royal line came the Messiah.
Neither Rahab nor Ruth earned God's mercy by possessing the right ancestry.
Their stories show that faith in the true God mattered more than the labels their nations carried.
And Bithiah?
We must leave the unknown parts of her life unknown.

Yet her recorded presence in Judah's genealogy stands beside these other accounts as a reminder that the Old Testament itself contains people from beyond Israel's borders within the story of God's covenant people.
Here is where the message becomes personal.
Some of us are comfortable believing God can save outsiders.
We just struggle to believe He can save people like us.
We can imagine Jesus forgiving a stranger.
But our own conscience keeps replaying the same scenes.
The betrayal.
The secret addiction.
The words we wish we could take back.
The marriage we damaged.
The person we hurt.
The years we wasted.
The compromises we justified.
The prayers we stopped praying because we felt too ashamed to approach God again.
And somewhere inside, a voice whispers:
You have gone too far.
But the Gospel does not tell you to measure the power of Christ's mercy by the size of your failures.
It tells you to look at the sufficiency of His sacrifice.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” — KJV
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we made ourselves worthy.
Not after we repaired every relationship.
Not after we developed a spotless reputation.
Christ died for sinners.
And His resurrection declares that death did not defeat Him.
This is why grace is more than a comforting religious word.
Grace is God's undeserved favor toward people who cannot rescue themselves.
It is not permission to continue deliberately in sin.
It is not a spiritual excuse to avoid repentance.
It is the mercy of God that brings salvation and teaches us to turn away from ungodliness.
Titus 2:11–12 joins those truths together.
The grace that saves is also the grace that trains us to live differently.
Jesus does not merely offer a better label for an unchanged life. He gives new life to those who belong to Him.
And perhaps that is the part of this message that hurts.
Because many of us want forgiveness without surrender.
We want peace without confession.
We want a new chapter while continuing to protect the sins that destroyed the previous one.
We want God to change our circumstances while refusing to let Him confront our hearts.
But Jesus did not come merely to decorate the old life.
He came to save us from sin.
He calls us to repent and believe the Gospel.
And repentance is not simply feeling terrible about what we have done.
It involves turning from sin toward God, trusting in Christ, and bearing fruit consistent with that change of heart.
It is possible to cry over the consequences of sin without truly surrendering the sin itself.
That is a difficult truth.
But sometimes the most loving thing we can hear is the truth that finally breaks our excuses.
Perhaps you have been attending church for years while quietly living a double life.
Perhaps your Bible remains unopened while your mind is filled with everything else.
Perhaps you know how to speak Christian language but have forgotten what it means to seek Christ in secret.
Perhaps you are respected publicly and spiritually exhausted privately.
And perhaps, right now, God is using a name buried in an ancient genealogy to draw your attention back to the question you have avoided.
Who truly has your heart?
Bithiah was identified as the daughter of an earthly ruler.
But the Gospel places a far greater invitation before us.
Through Christ, we can belong to the eternal King.
Not by bloodline.
Not by wealth.
Not by reputation.
Not by religious performance.
But through the grace of God received by faith.
Listen to the language of Ephesians 2:12–13.
Paul describes Gentile believers as people who were once strangers to the covenants of promise and without hope apart from God.
Then comes the turning point.
“But now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ.” — Ephesians 2:13, KJV
Made nigh.
Brought near.
Not because the distance was imaginary.
Not because sin was insignificant.
But because Jesus Christ accomplished what we could never accomplish for ourselves.
The cross is where God's justice and mercy meet.
Our sin is not brushed aside as though it never mattered.
Christ bore the penalty of sin, and those who trust in Him receive forgiveness and reconciliation with God.
This is the center of the story.
Not Pharaoh.
Not a palace.
Not even Bithiah.
Jesus Christ.
The One who left the glory of heaven and entered our broken world.
The One who welcomed repentant sinners while confronting religious hypocrisy.
The One who was rejected, mocked, crucified, buried, and raised from the dead.
The One whose blood purchased redemption.
The One who still calls sinners to come to Him.
And this is why the theme of Gospel Warrior is more than a memorable phrase.
Not because every scandal ends in earthly applause.
Not because every broken relationship will be restored exactly as we wish.
Not because following Christ guarantees a painless future.
But because Jesus can change a person's standing before God, forgive their sins, transform their heart, and give their life an eternal hope that their past could never provide.
That is the rewriting that matters most.
A person condemned by sin can be justified through faith.
A stranger can become a member of God's household.
A life once ruled by darkness can begin walking in the light.
A heart once hardened against God can be made new.
And a sinner who once fled from the truth can finally come into the light and say:
Lord Jesus, I need You.
There is another detail about Bithiah that deserves our attention.
Her name is preserved in a genealogy.
Not in a long biography.
Not in a dramatic speech.
Not in a chapter devoted entirely to her achievements.
Just a name, a family connection, and a remarkable identification.
We often imagine significance in terms of how much attention the world gives us.
How many people recognize us.
How many applaud us.
How many remember our accomplishments.
But Scripture reminds us that the world's measurements of significance are not God's measurements.
Bithiah's presence in the biblical record does not tell us how famous she was in her lifetime.
It does not tell us whether she was admired, opposed, or forgotten by those around her.
What it does tell us is that her name was included in the sacred record.
And that should make us consider the question of what kind of legacy we are building.
Because one day, the things we chased so desperately will no longer matter in the way we imagined.
The expensive possessions.
The titles.
The applause.
The online attention.
The arguments we insisted on winning.
The image we worked so hard to maintain.
All of it is temporary.
But our relationship with God has eternal significance.
Jesus asked in Mark 8:36:
“For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?” — KJV
That question has never lost its power.
You can have a palace and still need salvation.
You can have influence and still be spiritually lost.
You can have religious knowledge and still need repentance.
You can have thousands of people following your life and still be running away from the One who gave you life.
And you can have very little in this world, yet possess something infinitely more precious through faith in Christ.
The forgiveness of sins.
Peace with God.
The promise of resurrection.
The hope of eternal life.
Perhaps this is the moment to stop asking whether people think your life looks successful.
And begin asking whether your life belongs to Jesus.
Because the most devastating tragedy is not being forgotten by the world.
It is gaining everything the world offers while remaining unreconciled to God.
And the greatest miracle is not having your name celebrated by millions.
It is having your name written in heaven.
Jesus told His disciples in Luke 10:20 to rejoice that their names were written in heaven.
What a different way to measure a life.
Not by the grandeur of an earthly family.
Not by public recognition.
But by belonging to God.
Bithiah's name may be translated “Daughter of Yahweh,” but her name alone cannot establish her eternal standing.
For us, Scripture makes the way of salvation clear.
Jesus Christ is the Savior.
And He calls us to come to Him in faith.
If you are reading this while carrying hidden guilt, do not confuse conviction with hopelessness.
The purpose of the Gospel is not to leave repentant sinners buried under condemnation.
It is to lead them to the Savior who is able to forgive and cleanse.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — KJV
Do not use that promise to minimize your sin.
Use it as a reason to stop hiding.
Come honestly.
Confess what you have done.
Turn from what is destroying you.
Trust in Jesus Christ.
And where your actions have harmed others, seek to make things right as far as you are able.
You do not have to pretend that your past was beautiful.
You do not have to call evil good.
You do not have to deny the wounds.
You can bring the truth into the light.
Because the Savior who died for sinners is not surprised by the sin you have been afraid to confess.
And His mercy is not too small for the person who comes to Him in genuine repentance and faith.
Maybe you are reading this as someone who has already trusted Christ, but your faith has become tired.
You still believe.
You still pray, sometimes.
You still open your Bible when you remember.
But your heart has been carrying battles nobody sees.
Then remember this.
The Christian life is not sustained by your ability to remain emotionally strong every day.
It is sustained by the faithfulness of the Lord who holds His people.
Return to His Word.
Return to prayer.
Return to fellowship with believers who will speak truth and love into your life.
Do not isolate yourself in shame.
Do not allow spiritual exhaustion to convince you that surrender is pointless.
Christ has not called you to manufacture strength apart from Him.
He has called you to abide in Him.
And perhaps someone else needs to hear that today.
A family member who has quietly walked away from church.
A friend who believes their failures have disqualified them from God's mercy.
A believer who is smiling in public but struggling in private.
Someone who has never truly understood why Jesus came.
Not merely to circulate another religious post, but because someone in your circle may need to encounter the Scriptures and hear the Gospel of grace.
And if this message has confronted something in your own heart, I want to invite you into a moment of honesty.
You do not have to expose private details or publicly confess something that should be handled with appropriate pastoral care, wisdom, and accountability.
Sometimes a few sincere words are enough to remind another struggling believer that they are not alone.
Not to glorify the darkness.
But to glorify the Savior.
Your testimony may encourage someone who is still afraid to believe that change is possible.
There may come a night when the old accusations return, when shame feels louder than grace, or when you need to remember what Scripture says about belonging to Christ.
Come back to these verses.
Read them in context.
Let the Word of God, not merely the emotion of this moment, shape what you believe.
Our desire is to keep pointing people toward Jesus Christ through Scripture, biblical teaching, repentance, grace, forgiveness, and the daily work of discipleship.
We also want to speak directly to those who have been quietly strengthened by this ministry and are wondering how they can help it continue.
Every meaningful work of Gospel ministry requires time, labor, resources, and people willing to stand behind it.
Articles must be researched and written.
Biblical teaching must be prepared.
Resources must be developed and maintained.
And the opportunity to reach more people brings real responsibilities.
It is a way of saying, “I want sound biblical encouragement and discipleship resources to keep reaching people who need them.”
Scripture does teach the importance of generous support for ministry.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — KJV
Notice those words.
Not grudgingly.
Or of necessity.
Christian giving should not be produced by guilt or pressure.
Those gifts cannot be bought.
Your giving should reflect prayerful stewardship, your responsibilities, and the needs of your local church and family.

These resources and products are not substitutes for Scripture or membership in a faithful local church. They are simply additional ways we hope to encourage biblical reflection, daily discipleship, and meaningful conversations about Jesus.
Those free resources are part of our desire to help believers grow deeper in their knowledge of Jesus Christ.
A single share can introduce someone to a passage they have never considered.
A sincere comment can encourage a struggling believer.
A conversation begun through an article can lead someone to open the Bible, ask questions, and seek Christ.
Our responsibility is to be faithful with the opportunities entrusted to us.
And that brings us back to the Egyptian princess.
Bithiah.
A woman whose name appears in only a brief passage.
A daughter of Pharaoh remembered within the genealogy of Judah.
A name commonly understood to mean “Daughter of Yahweh.”
There are many things about her that we will never know from the biblical text.
But there is one thing we can know with certainty from the whole counsel of Scripture.
God's redemptive purpose is greater than human pride, earthly power, national boundaries, and the shame of our sinful past.
And the fullest revelation of that mercy is not found in a royal marriage recorded in Chronicles.
It is found at Calvary.
Where Jesus Christ gave Himself for sinners.
Where the righteous Savior died for the unrighteous to bring us to God.
Where the hope of forgiveness was secured through His sacrifice.
And where the story did not end in death, because on the third day He rose again.
So if you have been measuring your worth by your family name, your mistakes, your reputation, or the approval of people, hear the invitation of the Gospel.
Come to Jesus.
Not because you deserve a new beginning.
But because He is merciful.
Not because your sins are small.
But because His saving work is sufficient.
Not because you can rewrite your own heart.
But because God gives new life through Christ.
And when you come to Him, do not merely ask for a better public story.
Ask for a transformed life.
A heart that loves truth.
A spirit that turns away from sin.
A faith that endures.
A life that glorifies the One who saved you.
Because one day, every earthly title will fade.
Every palace will become dust.
Every human reputation will pass away.
And the question that matters will not be whether the world knew your name.
It will be whether you belonged to Jesus Christ.
The world may remember where you came from. But through Jesus Christ, your past does not have to be the final word about where you will spend eternity.
